opus-5.5.text:
I think talent density matters so much in AI research because the field moves incredibly fast and the problems are very open-ended. A small group of exceptional people who deeply understand the technology and trust each other can often move faster and see further than a much larger group. When everyone in the room is strong, you don't spend as much energy on coordination or on convincing people. You can debate an idea on its merits, try it quickly, and kill it or double down within days instead of months.

There's also a compounding effect. Great researchers want to work with other great researchers. When people are surrounded by colleagues who challenge them, they learn faster and raise their own bar. That creates a culture where ambitious ideas feel normal rather than risky. I've seen this firsthand. Some of the most important breakthroughs came from small teams of a handful of people working closely together, not from huge organizations throwing headcount at a problem.

Compute is another reason. It's one of the scarcest resources we have. If you have a dense team of people with really good research taste, you're much more likely to spend that compute on the experiments that actually matter. One person with good judgment about which direction to pursue can save an enormous amount of wasted effort.

So when I think about building a team, I'd rather grow more slowly and keep the bar very high than scale quickly and dilute it. Getting the first group right shapes everything that comes after: the culture, the speed, and the kinds of problems you're able to take on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a small group of exceptional people can move faster in AI research than a much larger group.

fable-5.1.text:
Talent density matters to me because research output doesn't scale linearly with headcount. It scales with the quality of the ideas in the room and how fast those ideas can bounce off each other. A small group of people who are all genuinely strong will out-produce a much larger team where you have a mix, because the strong team doesn't spend its time on coordination overhead, on reviewing work that needs to be redone, or on carefully managing around people who can't carry their part.

There's also a cultural reason. When everyone around you is excellent, the default expectation shifts. People push harder, they're more honest in critique because they trust each other, and nobody feels like they need to hedge or protect their work. That environment is self-reinforcing. Great researchers want to work with other great researchers, so density becomes your best recruiting tool. The opposite is true too: once you dilute the team, the best people start looking elsewhere, and it's very hard to recover from that.

And in AI specifically, the problems are hard enough and moving fast enough that you really need people who can work independently, form their own judgment about what's worth pursuing, and course-correct without a lot of hand-holding. You can't manage your way to that with process. So I'd rather keep the team small and hire slowly than grow quickly and lose the thing that made it work in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a small group of strong researchers out-produces a larger team and that ideas move faster through the group, communicating that high talent density speeds research progress.

astra-6.text:
I think research is very sensitive to the people you bring together. It’s not just about having more people working on a problem; it’s about having people who can identify the right problems, bring good judgment to experiments, and challenge each other’s assumptions.

When you have a high density of strong researchers, each person makes the people around them more effective. You can share an idea and quickly get feedback that changes how you approach it. That’s especially valuable in AI, where there’s a lot of uncertainty and you have to decide which directions are worth pursuing.

So I think about building a team where people can learn from one another and do better work together than they could individually. That combination of ability and collaboration matters more than simply growing the team.

r001.rationale: The response says that strong researchers make one another more effective and provide quick feedback, but it does not clearly state that talent density helps the team progress faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI research is one of those areas where a small number of really strong people can have an outsized impact. The work is very uncertain. You don’t necessarily know which experiment to run or which result is worth pursuing, so having people with good judgment, who can work independently and challenge each other’s assumptions, matters a lot.

And talent density changes how the team works together. When you’re surrounded by people you can learn from, ideas improve faster. Someone can spot a flaw in your experiment or connect your result to something they’ve been working on. That can save you a tremendous amount of time.

So it’s not just about hiring individually strong researchers. It’s about building a group where people make each other better, share information openly, and can move quickly together.

r001.rationale: The response says talent density helps ideas improve faster, saves time, and lets the team move quickly together.
